subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce tabled the order in council concerning Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. Apparently there also were agreements between some department of the government and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, or between Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation and the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. I wonder whether the minister would also table such agreement or agreements.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext:
When the documents left my office the agreement affecting Trans-Canada Pipe Lines was tabled with the order in council. I think the hon. member will find that the Clerk has both documents, but if not I will be glad to furnish anything which has been prepared and not tabled.
While I am speaking on this subject I might say that the financing of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines has now been approved by the conservation board of the province of Alberta and by the board of transport commissioners as well as by the government of Canada. So I think we can assume that that subject need not be pursued further.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: On that subject, would the minister say whether last year, when I understand there was a new agreement following the steel strike in the United States, the deadline for construction to Winnipeg was extended, and, if so, to what date; or was it simply lifted without any definite date being set?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: There was no new agreement after the steel strike in the United States. The only agreement which had been made affecting the western portion provided for protection against force majeure, and if the cost of the line is not repaid before the due date, which, I think, is April 2, the question as to whether force majeure occurred would be interesting; but as we are quite sure that the advances will be repaid shortly, the matter is purely academic.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Am I not right in understanding that the agreement provided for construction to Winnipeg by December 31, 1956, in the absence of strikes or something which rendered supplies unavailable? Surely a deadline was written into the agreement. Was that deadline extended to another date or was the company relieved of any obligation to meet the deadline with respect to construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: No, the company was not relieved of obligation to meet the deadline, but the obligation can be discharged under the agreement by the repayment of the government loan, and it will be discharged in that way.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: So there is some deadline by which the company is obliged to complete construction to Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Or by paying back their debts to the government.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext:
May I
ask a supplementary question with regard to the proposed public financing. Has the minister considered whether the proposed offering of bonds and common shares in a package, or unit, complies with the agreement of the Trans-Canada company to make a public offering in Canada of common shares?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Yes, sir, the common shares are being offered in Canada and considerably more than half the total of the outstanding shares will have been offered in Canada when the financing is complete.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: The reason I asked whether the minister had considered this matter is because I understand the public offering would be an offering of bonds and shares, whereas the agreement called for the offering of common shares. Presumably, common shares cannot be purchased alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: That is true, but the agreement nevertheless calls for an offer of shares in Canada, and shares are being offered.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: On condition you buy bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: What difference does that make?

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext:
It amounts to a condition of sale.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: There was no offer of that kind in any agreement. It was a verbal understanding with the group that represented the ownership of the pipe line, which I conveyed to the house. The understanding was that after the financing had been completed more than one-half of the total outstanding shares would have been offered to purchasers in Canada; and I may say, from reports reaching me, that all those shares will be taken up by purchasers in Canada, and I am satisfied the demand for further shares will still exist.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: May I take it that the minister considers what is being offered as in compliance with the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the fact that the agreement of May 8, 1956, clearly provides that the Trans-Canada company undertook to build the western section of the line by December 31, 1956, why has the company been relieved of all obligations with respect to a deadline for the completion of this section of the line and the only obligation remaining is to repay the loan? How could they just be relieved of that obligation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, possibly if the government had wished to acquire the western section under the terms of the mortgage and had wished to foreclose the mortgage, they could have attempted to declare the company in default. I think the company would have had a good defence because, as everyone knows, the cause of their default was that a steel strike in the United States had interfered with the delivery of pipe into western Canada for a period of about two and a half months. However, the government has not claimed default and, as I say, the company can discharge all claims of the government of Canada by the repayment of the money that was advanced to the company for the western section.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: My question is, why was not a new deadline established? Granted, for the sake of argument, that we agree with the statement, why did you not negotiate a new deadline instead of lifting all obligations with respect to a deadline?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext:
We lifted no obligations and we set no new deadline. We wanted to reserve the position if at any time we desired to contest the position of the company as being in default, we would base
IMr. Fulton.]
our default claim on the original agreement. No new agreement was made and no agreement was lifted.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: The company is in default? Is the company in default?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext:
You say so. Let
the courts say whether you are right.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: How can it not be in default under the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: That is a matter for the courts to decide, namely to what extent the force majeure provision remedied the apparent default.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: The courts cannot decide after the order in council was passed last Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Would you like us to declare the company in default? I know you are trying to kill this pipe-line project-

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: That old canard will not get you anywhere.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: -instead of taking the logical step which will permit it to be completed on time.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Is that why you made the order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Certainly, that is why we made the order in council. We wanted our money back and the pipe line built.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: It was wholly improper to have made the order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: I am glad to hear that legal opinion from the leader of a great party, and I will remember it.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: In view of the fact that parliament was told last summer that the bill had to go through by June 7 in order that construction could be completed by a certain date, and construction was not completed by that date, why has the government not held the company in default when construction was not completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext:
The reason that the bill had to go through by a certain date was so that the company would be justified in undertaking the building of the line under the then agreement. That was the agreement with the company which was prevailing at that time. As I say, if we had preferred ownership of that uncompleted pipe line to the return of the money advanced by the government we might have gone into the courts and tried to enforce default against

the company. We are anxious to have a pipe line completed from Alberta to Montreal. In spite of all the efforts to prevent it from across the house we believe that the project will be completed, and completed by autumn of 1958.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: No matter how many times they break their word you will do nothing about it.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was going to ask an overall question. Is there any doubt in the mind of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this pipe line is not going to go through? Is there any doubt, anywhere, east or west? I think that should end it if we get a good answer.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: There is no answer.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited has ever met any deadline that was set for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Yes, the pipe line met the deadline of satisfying the government that the pipe line has finances and that it is able and willing to pay back the advances relating to the western section by April 2, 1957. That deadline will be met.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: How did they meet that deadline?

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: I would like to ask-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: I would like an answer. How many extensions had the company been given before they met that deadline?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the document giving that information was tabled yesterday. The order in council sets it all out in detail. If my hon. friend has not read the order in council he is not as well prepared as usual. Perhaps he has read it and knows the answer himself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    REQUEST FOR TABLING OF AGREEMENTS    ACTION OF GOVERNMENT ON FINANCING

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Would the minister comment on the charge by Mrs. John Gorman, legal counsel for the Alberta Indian association, as reported in this morning's Globe and Mail, that the action of the minister in holding up a petition directed to the Queen is an act contrary to British justice and a denial of the right of subjects to petition Her Majesty in a case where it is felt an injustice is being done and solemn Indian treaties of the 1870's are being broken by representatives of the Queen? Will the minister indicate whether or not he will send that petition to Her Majesty, to whom it is addressed, and also by what authority the petition was transferred from the Governor General's office to him?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have said once or twice before in the house that I did not think it would be wise for a minister of the crown to give legal opinions of his own in the house.

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: Would the minister advise the house of the number of petitions and resolutions he has received protesting the Hobbema Indian reserve action from home and school associations, church organizations, bar societies and other groups of conscientious Canadians, and will he advise the house of the nature of his replies to each of the three or four specific requests for amendment of the 1951 Indian Act and Indian policy in general contained in these resolutions and petitions?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: What subject are you debating now?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext:
I do not think I can give offhand the number I have received. It is quite considerable. As to the second part of the question, I have given the same answer to these petitions as I have given in the house, namely, that a procedure was laid down by parliament for an appeal to the courts and I think it would be a very extraordinary thing to change that law in the midst of a proceeding and to deny to those who now have an appeal to the courts the appeal that was given to them by parliament. I repeat what I have said before, that there is an opportunity of appeal to the courts provided by parliament, that it seems to me that advantage should be taken of that opportunity, and it seems to me it would be a very wrong thing and,

indeed, rather contemptuous of parliament, to attempt to interfere in any way with that.
I should like to add one other thing. There seems to be a misapprehension that the act of 1951 changed the definition of an Indian. Those hon. members who are lawyers know perfectly well that it did nothing of the kind. No change whatsoever was made in the definition of an Indian by the act of 1951. All it did was to provide legal procedure for determining in certain cases any dispute as to whether a particular person was or was not an Indian. But the law setting out those who are Indians and those who are not Indians still is the law that was in existence at the time this reserve was set up. What is being suggested by the representations that have come to me is that people that some persons allege are squatters on the reserve and have no rights to share in the trust-

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: After 60 years?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext:
-should by an act of
parliament be given a share of the trust. That is what the proposition is. If these people are Indians according to the definition which existed at the time the reserve was set up they are entitled to remain on the reserve. If they are not Indians but people whose ancestors squatted on the reserve, the fact that they have been there for a long time does not, as I apprehend it, change the legal situation. It seems to me that until this matter can be brought before a competent court and settled we should not be discussing it here.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister whether, in view of the three judgments handed down by courts in Saskatchewan recently, he will reconsider the statement he made a moment ago that the 1951 amendments did not have the effect of changing the meaning of the word "Indian"? I refer to the three judgments given by district court judges within the last few weeks in connection with appeals launched by Indians whose names were erased from the band membership.
Second, I should like to ask the minister this question. In view of the fact that so-called squatters-to use his expression-had in many cases been on the lands of the reserve without challenge for 50 years or 60 years, does he not feel that common justice to these poor unfortunate people demands an amendment at once if the law be what he says it is?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext:
If I might answer the second question first, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. It does not seem to me that if the hon.

gentleman's grandfather had had a farm and if he had tolerated someone living on that farm for a long time, it would be an appropriate thing for parliament in our day to pass a statute giving half that farm to the descendant of the person that he and his family had tolerated living on it for that time. That is what his suggestion amounts to. As for the judgments of the courts in Saskatchewan, as I understand it the judgments of the courts in Saskatchewan reversed the registrar. That is why there is an appeal, namely so that the registrar's decision can be considered. If the courts in Saskatchewan reversed the registrar, it will be quite open to the courts in Alberta to do exactly the same thing if there is the same evidence. It does not seem to me that it is proper for me or for anyone here to attempt in advance to prejudge the decision which this parliament, not I, left to the courts.

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I just ask the minister this question. Is it not a fact that in Saskatchewan where appeals took place-three of them in three different judicial districts-the judges held that the provisions of the act of 1951 did not apply to those who were on the reserves prior to the date on which the statute was passed? If I am correct in my premise, then why does the minister not end this tyranny in the Hobbema reserve on the basis of these judgments which apparently the minister is not going to appeal and which, unless they are followed by Alberta, will result in the law being interpreted in one way in Saskatchewan and in another way in Alberta?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, do you not think that we ought to wait until the courts in Alberta have interpreted it in order to see whether that situation would arise which the hon. gentleman is attempting to forecast as the decision of the courts in Alberta?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext:
May I
ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. From whom did he receive the legal advice that the definition of an Indian, as contained in the 1951 amendment, did not change the previous definition of an Indian? Is he aware that at the time the ancestors of these Indians who are now being expelled from the Hobbema and other reserves settled on those reserves the definition of an Indian was anyone who followed the Indian way of life?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext:
I should think, sir, that as to the first question my reply would be that the advice I received was advice from the appropriate officer of my department. As
Inquiries of the Ministry to the second question, I would not venture to give an opinion without consulting the documents.

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Will he please answer specifically that portion of my question asked earlier which had nothing whatsoever to do with any legal action under way in Canada at the present time? In other words, by whose authority was the Indians' petition to the Queen transferred from the office of the Governor General to himself? Furthermore, will the minister please indicate whether he will send this petition on to Her Majesty to whom it is addressed?

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: I answered that question yesterday when I indicated that I was seeking advice on this subject.

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that we are met with an adamant refusal on the part of the minister to do anything in connection with these unfortunate Indians, I intend to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Would he consider looking into this matter and in the meantime giving a stay of proceedings in so far as the eviction of these Indians is concerned? Will he also give consideration to setting up a royal commission to determine the rights of these people who may not have votes but who have the right to consideration by this parliament?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I should answer the question just put by the Leader of the Opposition in any way that would commit the government. It may be a very popular cause at this time to try to make much out of the unfortunate situation in which some of those find themselves who have been found to be residing on this reserve and not to be Indians. However, there are legal proceedings that can be taken and should be taken and which I hope will be taken. If they are not taken they can be supplemented by action recommended to this parliament to see that there is consideration by the courts of the question of fact involved in this matter.
This is something which was apparently not considered of very much importance by anyone until a very greatly enhanced value was given to the lands of this reserve by the oil finds either on it or in the surrounding territory. Proprietary rights are now involved and I think they should be decided by the courts, as is always the case.
I have not gone into all the facts but the information I have is that the definition of

Inquiries of the Ministry who is or who is not an Indian entitled to be on the reserve has remained unchanged over the whole time since that reserve was set up. There was a procedure instituted under the act of 1951 to have the question of fact tested if there was a contest as to who had or who had not the right to be treated as an Indian on the Indian reserve. That procedure involved an investigation by commissioners, then a finding by the registrar which was subject to appeal to the district court.
As the hon. gentleman has stated, there have been three cases in the province of Saskatchewan where after investigation and a finding on the investigation by the registrar the courts have found that the registrar's finding was wrong and quashed it. There is nothing to suggest that the district court would now confirm or quash a finding of the registrar in this case, but it is the district court which has been given by parliament the responsibility of doing that. I do not think it would be proper when there is a dispute about proprietary rights to attempt to set up a royal commission to make a decision on that dispute instead of having it decided by the ordinary courts of the country.

subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA
speechtext: Does the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration believe he is holding a pretty hot potato when he delays for 24 hours a message sent to Her Majesty the Queen by her subjects; when he takes over 24 hours to get some legal advice on diverting a petition to Her Majesty? Who is he? Who is the gentleman who dares to do that?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SITUATION ON HOBBEMA

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO ADVERTISE- MENT IN "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice I received from my hon. friend of his question, for which I thank him, is divided into two parts and I should prefer to answer the second part of it first. That was as to whether or not the federal

Department of Justice is concerned about the testing of possible infractions of the Criminal Code.
Of course the Department of Justice is always interested in the results of criminal proceedings in the courts, particularly from the standpoint as to whether these results disclose the need for amendments to the Criminal Code which it is the responsibility of the Department of Justice to recommend to the government and to parliament. But as I have stated on many occasions in the past-and apparently from this question that is now asked, it should be restated-the responsibility under our constitutional system for the enforcement of the criminal law rests with the provincial attorneys general.
It is for this reason that, in reply to my hon. friend's first question as to whether or not the two full pages of advertisements in this morning's Globe and Mail are violations of section 179 of the Criminal Code, I would point out first that traditionally the Minister of Justice does not express legal opinions in parliament; and second, that if he did so, I cannot see that there would be any purpose in his expressing a legal opinion in respect of an alleged offence which it is the responsibility of the provincial attorney general to prosecute. In the third place, I would not wish to express any kind of opinion at all with respect to these advertisements until I had before me a detailed police report of the complete set of facts upon which crown counsel would have to rely in any prosecution based upon such advertisement.

I told the hon. gentleman that I thought the editorial and the article spoke for themselves-that there was no one in this house who would not conclude, having followed these events, that I have been interested in this matter from the first and that the government had given every indication, by the initiative it has taken, that it, too, was interested in the matter of hospital insurance.
The government is, of course, not "hedging" in any way. The hon. gentleman has given this matter a great deal of study, and he knows it is very important in all questions of this kind that before we embark upon agreed procedures we clearly understand what we are seeking to do. The important thing to keep in mind is what the federal offer means to Ontario and to other provinces. It means, for Canada as a whole, that the federal government will be meeting half the cost of standard ward care, laboratory and radiological services for all persons in the population who are brought within the scheme.
The federal government, together with, I am sure, every hon. member who has studied this matter, wishes to see everyone possible brought within the scheme in order that the reduced charges which are made possible by this generous offer-and that is what it is-may be made effective for our people. We do not want to see a situation develop in any province where only a small portion of the population is covered and the rest are not. In such a situation, while the federal expenditure would be proportionately reduced, the result would be far from satisfactory. The population covered under the federal proposal would be receiving hospitalization at a greatly reduced cost as a result of the federal contribution, while the population not covered would have to go on as before, meeting the full cost of its hospital care.
I indicated previously in this house, following the tabling of the plan by the premier of Ontario, that I had every reason to be optimistic and that I felt it would prove possible for the premier and the government of Ontario, after negotiations which are necessary in a matter of this sort, to bring their plan within the principles envisaged

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canada Elections Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill No. 5, which is identical with a bill I had the privilege of presenting to the house last year, is to extend the privilege of voting at advance polls in federal elections so that that privilege may be enjoyed by any qualified elector who finds that he will be absent from his home constituency on election day. Hon. members who may have looked at the bill, either last year or this year, will recognize that it is a document of some nine pages and that there might seem to be quite a few details in it. Let me make it perfectly clear that all the other changes in the act proposed in Bill No. 5 are purely consequential changes arising out of the change with regard to voting at advance polls.
I wish also to make it clear that the particular changes suggested by my bill consequential upon that major change are not sacrosanct. I mean by that that it would be quite satisfactory so far as I am concerned if the details of those consequential changes were altered by a committee after second reading of the bill. What is important in the bill and in any event what one should stick to in speaking to its second reading is its main principle, which is to make it possible
[Mr. Robertson.!
for any qualified elector in a federal election to vote at an advance poll if he finds that he will be away from home on election day.
As hon. members are aware, the Canada Elections Act as it now stands makes provision for advance polls but the right to vote at those advance polls is limited to a very few categories of Canadian citizens. The only ones who may vote at advance polls are commercial travellers, fishermen, employees on railways, vessels, aircraft and so on, who in the course of their duties are required to be away from home on election day, together with members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I think all members will agree that one of the most common grievances drawn to our attention at election time, and all of us in this place have had experience with elections, is the fact that many ordinary people who find they will be away from home on election day cannot vote at an advance poll. It is particularly annoying to voters to discover that they cannot vote at an advance poll when they are aware of the fact that an advance poll does exist. This strikes those so denied that right as a form of discrimination, and I am sure all of us can tell stories of many protests that arise with regard to this matter at every election.
There is another way in which it seems to me there is a form of discrimination with respect to this matter. It arises from the fact that when a general election is held in the summertime, and most of our elections are held in the summer months, there are always people who are away on holidays at that particular time. Some people can afford to return to their homes for election day in order to cast their vote. Others who happen to be away for their holidays during a period that runs over election day cannot afford to make the trip home, and there again one comes up against a feeling of discrimination.
Not only because grievances of this kind should in my view be met, not only because any element of discrimination should, if at all possible, be removed, but because the bill is in line with the basic principle underlying the establishment of the franchise in a democratic country do I feel that it should be supported by the House of Commons. That basic principle in a democracy is that the right to vote should not be restricted but rather should be made available to as wide a group of our citizens as possible, and if one is going to carry out that principle barriers such as this should be removed.
Let us tell ourselves, as has often been said when the elections act is under discussion in parliament, that the matter of voting is not something that belongs to us

because we happen to be in parliament. It does not belong to the government. It does not even belong to parliament. It is a right that belongs to the people of Canada. Our only job on their behalf is to make sure that the law governing that right to vote is as fair, generous and democratic as it can possibly be. So long as some of our citizens on election day, because they find they will have to be away from home, are denied the right to vote whereas some other citizens away from home on election day get the right to vote there is this feeling that there is unfairness and discrimination. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge that consideration be given to the principle of this bill which, as I say, would make it possible for any qualified elector away from home on election day to vote at an advance poll.
I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to violate the rule which I myself quoted a moment ago concerning the requirement that discussion on second reading relate only to the principle of the bill. However, I might perhaps point out some of the details of the bill which, of course, flow from this general change. For example, if more persons are going to be permitted to vote at the advance poll than is now the case, it would obviously be necessary to hold the advance poll a little further ahead of the general election day than is now the case.
My bill makes such a provision. The particular provision that my bill makes, as I have already indicated, is not sacrosanct. That provision can be changed. I mention that point simply to express the hope that hon. members will not take a stand in opposition to the bill merely because there is in its mechanics some detail with which they disagree. I for one would be quite happy in the committee on privileges and elections, if this bill is referred to that committee, to see any change made in mechanics of that kind. The same comment goes for the change as to the date of nomination made necessary in order to facilitate the taking of an advance poll amongst more voters than is the case at the present time.
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that this privilege of voting at advance polls on a universal basis already obtains in some of our provinces with respect to their provincial elections. Most of the provinces have some advance poll privileges but in several of the eastern provinces, at any rate, those privileges are restricted along lines similar to the restrictions that are still in the Canada Elections Act. But in the four western provinces-I refer to British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba-there are provisions for voting at advance polls by any 82715-53J
Canada Elections Act
qualified voter who finds that he has to be away from home on election day. As a matter of fact, even more generous provision is made in two of the western provinces, unless British Columbia has changed it; I have not been able to ascertain whether or not they have done so in recent changes in the election act. With that qualification I say that in two of the western provinces, namely British Columbia and Saskatchewan, even more generous provision is made in that there is absentee voting so that persons who are away from home can vote on election day in the constituency in the province where they happen to be on that day. In the case of Saskatchewan both absentee voting and universal voting at advance polls is provided. So far as Manitoba and Alberta are concerned, there is no provision for absentee voting but the right to vote at advance polls is universal. In other words, any person who is a qualified elector and who finds he must be away from home on election day may vote at the advance poll.
Some of those who have not been too sure whether they can support my bill have thought that maybe its provisions were too wide and that maybe it makes it too easy to vote at the advance poll. May I point out that my bill makes it not quite as easy to vote at an advance poll as is the case in provincial elections in my own province of Manitoba. I quote my own province of Manitoba to my friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard), who no doubt will speak on this matter, because after all it is the only province on the mainland of Canada with a Liberal government. I am therefore sure that he would be interested in the provisions there.
In Manitoba all that is necessary for a qualified voter to vote at the advance poll is to appear in person before a returning officer and obtain a certificate. No affidavit is required. All that is required is simply a personal appearance. Form 19 which is included in the election act in my province simply provides for the returning officer to issue that certificate to any qualified voter who merely appears before him in person. In the case of my bill, it goes at least a little further in that, in order to obtain the right to vote at an advance poll, a voter must not only appear in person before the returning officer but must take an affidavit to the effect that he has reason to believe that he will be away from home on the general election day. I think that is a sufficient protection against abuse of the privilege. I think it is sufficient protection against people voting at the advance poll if it is not necessary for them to do so.

Canada Elections Act
In, another debate on this matter the Secretary of State expressed the fear that if advance polls were open to all voters the number of people voting at advance polls would mount until it might exceed the number left to vote on general election day. I still make the point with him-and I hope he accepted it when I made it last year-that it is rather hard to argue in that way when, in any of the provinces where universal voting at advance polls is allowed, there is no experience that would support that idea. In my own province of Manitoba, as in the other western provinces, those who require to vote at advance polls in provincial elections do so, but percentagewise their number is still very small. Nevertheless, the fact that the right is there removes this grievance that is felt very keenly at election time by so many people. That indeed was one of the principal arguments advanced last year by the Secretary of State, namely the feeling that this provision would lead to several election days rather than one main election day. If I thought there was any substance in that fear I certainly would have to give some weight to it. But I suggest to him that he should take note of the experience in the provinces where we have universal voting at advance polls, and that if he does so he will see that that fear is really quite unfounded.
Another objection voiced last year was that made by my friend the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert) who also spoke against this bill. He criticized my proposal on the ground that, if my bill went through, it would be possible for people who were just going away on trips or people who were just going away on holidays to vote at the advance polls. Let there be no secret about it, Mr. Speaker. That is one of the purposes of the bill. Surely, it is not a crime to go away on a holiday. Surely, that is not something that should cost one his right to vote or cost him any of his rights of citizenship. Holidays are becoming more and more general. They will be more general still if certain bills of mine receive favourable consideration before this session is over. At any rate, it is now accepted as part of our life in this country that people should have an annual vacation, and should have it with pay as well, Mr. Speaker.
Also, it is becoming fairly general for our elections to be held during the summer months. If one goes back over quite a number of years, but for the winter election of 1940, one finds that all of our federal elections have been held in what might be called the summer months. I should think there is no doubt but that the general election this year will be held in one of the

summer months. At the moment, it looks as though it will be either in the month of May or the month of June; certainly, it will come no later than June 17.

As I say, I believe it will be on May 27 or in the month of June; certainly not later than June 17.
One or two other objections were raised last year. One that was put up by one of my friends to the right was the extra cost that might be involved in providing for these extra advance polls. Of course, one could use that argument against the franchise generally, that it is a costly business. But surely, it is one of the most beneficial expenditures that we make in a democracy, namely any expenditure that is made to provide for the people to express their views freely as to those whom they want to represent them in parliament.
Some objection was raised in one quarter last year as to whether a provision of this kind might open the way to a greater amount of impersonation at election time. From the experience in my part of the country, that is not a fear that I entertain. The act is well drawn in that respect, in terms of preventing fraud and impersonation. I have tried in this bill to add any additional precautions that are necessary in connection with this further right so that there will not be fraud or impersonation.
In connection with the drafting of this bill, I should like once again to express my thanks to Dr. Maurice Ollivier, our parliamentary counsel, and Mr. Nelson Castonguay, the chief electoral officer, for the help they gave me something over a year ago in preparing this bill. I want to make it quite clear again, as I did last year, that in mentioning their names it does not mean they are either for or against the principle of the bill. It was a real help to have their assistance in putting

in concrete form the changes that would be necessary to carry out this principle.
Mr. Speaker, this right to vote is the property of the Canadian people and not something that belongs to us here in parliament. I feel it should be made as widely available as possible, without any barriers such as the real barrier that is there when some people have to be away from home on election day. I hope that the house will give favourable consideration to this bill, and I hope that it will vote for second reading so that the bill can be referred to a committee where we can make any changes in the mechanics that may be necessary. Nevertheless let us now write into our election law the basic principle that everyone who is a qualified voter should have a right to vote at an advance poll if he finds he will be away from home on election day.

As I said before, I intend to be very brief because I do not feel it would be proper for me to repeat the arguments against the adoption of this measure which I advanced last year. I think the fact remains that, in my opinion, the main argument to be put forward in opposition to the measure resides in the fact that, as the hon. member indicated himself when he referred to what I said last year, if we allow a multiplication of these advance polls you will defeat the main purpose of the act which is to permit the Canadian people to choose their representatives in this house on one specified date. In other words, if one reads the Canada Elections Act and studies it carefully, he must come to the conclusion that all the sections of the act converge upon one main event which is polling day itself.
The hon. member said that, under the act as it now stands, there are very few people who are authorized to vote at an advance poll. I admit that, and I say that there are very few because they have to be exceptions to the general rule and there have to be very serious reasons to justify the electors of Canada not to take advantage of that one occasion they have every four or five years to freely choose the men or women they wish to represent them in parliament. I feel that if we were to multiply these advance polls, if we
Canada Elections Act
were to accept the very wide proposal put forward by my hon. friend that whoever believes he is going to be away on polling day will be able to cast his vote at an advance poll, then I am sure the result would be that a great many would vote at such advance poll. Last year, my hon. friend said he thought this argument was absurd. He said the suggestion was absurd because that had not happened in his province.
I do not know exactly when these advance polls were established in his province, but one thing is certain. If you allow a greater number of people to vote at the advance polls, if you tell them they do not have to concern themselves about being in their constituencies on election day but they will be entitled to vote on two or three days other than on polling day, then a great number will take advantage of that privilege. Surely the number will increase. Will it increase to the extent some day of having more people voting on these other polling days than on polling day itself? I do not know, but one may suspect and may have reason to believe that eventually the interest in polling day itself will be completely lost. In other words, is it not a true contention that there might be more people voting at these advance polls? I submit that you could have the result of having fewer people voting on polling day itself because they will say, "We have the opportunity to vote on three or four different days" and the interest of the electors will be lost, in my opinion, in the very day on which they have to make their choice.
My hon. friend has referred to the delay between nomination day and polling which, under the proposal, will be extended to 21 days. He thinks that 21 days should be allowed instead of 14 days. So far as I am concerned, the 14 days that do exist under the act are very important for the electors to form a judgment as to whom they are going to choose to represent them in parliament. In other words, if the elector is going to be away, as the proposal suggests, during the nine days, if he is going to be away on his holidays-it is true he has a right to have his holidays-nobody will contest that, but is it not a fact that he should, when he knows that arrangements are made long in advance and election day has been announced a long time before, feel that it is his obligation, if he wants to have the privilege, to see to it that he is well informed as to the candidates who are running in the election so that he can form a sound judgment and make a proper choice? In other words, I am trying to make the point as clear as I can that we should not destroy the significance of polling day as being the one day under the act when an election is to be held, and that we should

not, by allowing other days to be used for the purpose, destroy the significance of polling day itself.

It is true that the matter of costs should not prompt us to decide against the principle underlined in this bill. It is true that the question of costs should not be sufficient for us to dispose of this matter and say, "Because it is going to be too costly we are going to vote against this bill." In some countries they have compulsory voting, something to which I am wholly opposed, but on the other hand if we are not going to have more and more people talking in terms of compulsory voting we must make every conceivable effort to make it possible for those who are qualified to be able to vote.

As to the suggestion that was made a moment ago about the advanced polling day-[DOT] making it three or four days instead of one- people might get that into their heads, and, instead of turning up on voting day, choose the next day to go to the polls. They might make arrangements, ahead of time, to go away on the regular voting day, and I believe that, in fairness to the voters and to hon. members of this house, this bill should be shelved at the present time and brought up in committee next year when the committee on elections would have an opportunity to call in witnesses and find out just what we could do about the proposals.

Reference was made this afternoon to the fact that the four western provinces have adopted some of these innovations and it was said that the four western provinces have set us such a good example that we in the federal field should do the same thing. In all earnestness I cannot honestly say that since the four western provinces adopted some of these new voting techniques we have had any more intelligent verdicts from the people of those provinces than we had under the old system. I for one am quite interested to note that while the present government of British Columbia came to power under one voting system it was not too long before it switched back to the old voting system. I notice that even my hon. friends of the Social Credit

group, who for so many years were so proud of the switched vote system, have now switched back to the good, old, tried, trusty and reliable one X system of British voting.
I for one do not believe that we should go overboard too quickly or introduce too many of these innovations. While I am quite frank to say that I would not have any objection to the bill because I do not think it would do any harm and might do a little good, nevertheless I think it would be costly and expensive and that the expense would probably outbalance the benefit.
There is one final point I wish to make. The most serious objection I see to my hon. friend's bill, having reflected about it since last year, is the provision whereby nomination day would be fixed even farther ahead of voting day than under the present system. I think that our election procedures in Canada are too long drawn out, too laborious and too expensive. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), for whom I have great respect, suggested that we might keep the general polls open for longer than one day. I think most of the expense of holding an election is centred right around one day now and if we kept the polls open for two days the expense would be twice as great. If we kept them open three days it would be three times as great.
I think our election techniques are now too expensive and long drawn out. I have had the great privilege in my professional capacity of having to cover British election campaigns. Certainly from my own experience I know that in the area that I represent in this house this question of people being disqualified in elections is one of great concern. I think perhaps Comox-Alberni district is as good an example of that fact as exists anywhere on the coast. In many cases if-as often happens-a large number of people in my district have to leave the place where they are working shortly before an election, they do not go to some other place within the electoral district but rather, if they are loggers or if they are fishermen, they find themselves going into a place like Vancouver. If I were having an opportunity to argue on the details of this bill in committee, I should like to suggest that provision be made, where circumstances warranted it, that electors could vote at an advance poll in another electoral district than the one in which they had been originally enumerated. Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this bill is of great importance to the people of my constituency. Of all the complaints one hears about the manner in which our elections are conducted the principal complaint is about discrimination. I am quite sure that other hon. members have had the same experience I have had of people saying: Why should I be discriminated against? I am not a railroader, I am not a commercial traveller, but in order to earn my living it is necessary for me to leave the city and travel perhaps 100 or 150 miles in order to perform the job which I am called upon to do and at a given time it may

be necessary for me to be away and thus miss the opportunity of voting.
I realize it is difficult to draw a line as to what classifications would be entitled to vote at an advance poll, but in a city like Regina there are many construction workers and other people who do contract work outside the city, such as wiring farm homes and so on. During the course of their jobs they find it necessary to be absent from the city on polling day. These people are very anxious to vote as they are fully cognizant of their responsibilities as citizens. It seems rather unfair that they should not be accorded the right to cast their votes the same as other employees who are provided for under the existing legislation.
While I agree that it is difficult to know where to draw a line, I think that is the best reason why we should accept this bill. The only way in which we are going to be able to treat all voters fairly is by making some realistic provision for voting at an advance poll. There has been some comment about possible difficulties. The minister suggested that people who are on holidays should return to vote and then, I presume, go back to resume their vacation. I will grant that when the election act was first placed on the statute books most people did not have automobiles and factory workers had no opportunity to travel very far afield. Consequently it might have been possible that there was a greater percentage of voters in their home localities at any given time. However, I think today, particularly in sparsely settled areas such as Saskatchewan, workers, when they get their holidays, are going to travel considerable distances to visit relatives or one or other of the many beauty spots throughout this country.
I have always believed we should encourage Canadians to travel. I am very pleased to note the great number of people from the prairies who visit British Columbia each year, and the great number from British Columbia who visit the prairie provinces. And I think it is a good thing that the prairie people should visit Ontario and the maritimes. That is possible when so many people are getting three weeks' holidays. In my province, at least, where all workers are provided with two weeks' paid holidays, they should be encouraged to visit other parts of Canada.
I think it is most unfair to say to such people, "Your holidays commence one week before election day, and if you want to vote you will have to curtail the extent of your travel in order to return to your home to do so." I think that is not the sort of thing we should expect under the electoral law of Canada, and I rather deplore any suggestion that these people are not aware of their
Canada Elections Act
responsibilities as citizens simply because they take their holidays at a given time. 1 think it is asking a great deal to expect someone to give up two weeks' holidays on account of an election, because that is what it amounts to. In my own province you cannot expect a person who travels, let us say, from Regina to Prince Albert national park to drive the considerable distance back to Regina, or Moose Jaw or some area in the southern part of the province, in order to cast a vote.
It seems to me we should be primarily concerned with getting the maximum number of people to vote in this country. I think we would all agree that the ideal situation would be that everyone should vote, and certainly we should place no obstacles in the path of any Canadian citizen who wishes to exercise his franchise. While there may be difficulties advanced and objections made to the present proposals, I think all these objections, if they went before the committee, could be ironed out and satisfactorily dealt with. I think the main question now, is simply this. Do we want to make it possible for a greater number of Canadian citizens to exercise their franchises? If we believe that is a desirable thing, then I think the most effective way of indicating our sincerity is to vote for the bill now before the house.

If there were any semblance of truth in this suggestion it would have shown itself in the province of British Columbia during the application of legislation which, I think, goes back either to 1920 or 1925. But the situation visualized by the minister has not developed.
I know. I ran as a provincial candidate in British Columbia in some seven elections, and I therefore recall very well what happened on polling day and how many ballots were cast at the advance and the absentee polls, and I can assure my hon. friends that in the seven elections which I contested provincially over a period of 20 years-and I represented one of the biggest constituencies in the province of British Columbia as far as population was concerned-there were never more than 500 votes cast in the advance or absentee ballots. That was not too large a number in comparison with the thousands who voted on polling day, but it was of great importance to the four or five hundred people who were able to vote because of the fact that there was provision to this effect.
The minister emphasized time after time that there had to be a sense of responsibility on the part of the elector himself, and nobody will disagree with that; but I think we should also emphasize the responsibility which the government has of ensuring that as many people as possible who will not be in their home constituencies on election day should have the opportunity of exercising their democratic right to vote.
This applies in particular to the province of British Columbia because, as the minister must know, the major industries of British Columbia are logging, mining, fishing and construction. As you realize, Mr. Speaker, in connection with all these enterprises in British Columbia there are always thousands on the move from logging camp to logging camp, from sawmill to sawmill. The people concerned cannot govern themselves so they are in their own ridings at a date set at the will of the Prime Minister. Our fishermen, sir, know that election day is set by the Prime Minister, but the days on which they can fish are established by the Department of Fisheries, and on the days they go out fishing they are away, as hon. members know, before sunrise, and they do not come back before the sun has set. away for days at a time. Why should these responsible citizens be denied the right to vote because their occupation does not allow them to be in their own constituencies on polling day?

In other words, a person goes in to vote at noon or in the afternoon, only to find that somebody has voted in his place, has stolen his name, has impersonated him. That is done and there is nothing that you can do about it.

I visualize, for instance, a city where there is a bit of skulduggery done, and we would say that at a couple of hundred polls three or four or half a dozen in each poll have voted previously on a declaration such as might be described in this resolution, and then we find that those declarations were spurious. A person comes along on election day only to find that he cannot vote because someone else has already voted and made this declaration. He says: "I did not make it." What can be done about that? That is the difficulty which I see here. I would like to support it, but I do not want anything like that to happen.

Of the other half, about 20 per cent have been somewhere on the high seas on voting day, either in the deep-sea trade, in the coastal trade or else fishing on the grand banks. Another 30 per cent have been out of the riding altogether, employed in other parts of Canada. I am not sure whether or not they were able to vote in the places where they were working.
This bill is therefore of considerable interest to my constituents. But I should like to say right at the beginning that I heartily agree with what the hon. member for Peterborough said earlier today, namely that this bill should not have been introduced at this particular time because I think it is going to confuse the issue.
As I have listened to the arguments put forward by the opposition side in favour of this bill I can see a great deal of confusion already. In the first place, we are confusing people's right to vote with the convenience of voting. Nobody is being deprived of the right to vote if there is no advance poll. Neither is a person given an additional right to vote by the creation of an advance poll. What the advance poll does is to give an extra convenience to the voters in that locality where it is established.
In my riding of Burin-Burgeo I have about
45.000	people, of whom about 20,000 are electors. Those 20,000 are distributed over
1.000	miles of coastline in about 250 different settlements. In most of those settlements there is a polling booth. Some of the smaller settlements are too small to have a voting booth, and the people must row by boat three or four miles to the nearest poll in order to vote. If the weather is bad and they cannot row that distance, then of course they do not vote. In some of the larger centres there may be five or six separate polling stations. Hence the total number of polling booths in my riding would be somewhere about 200 or 220. I have mentioned these figures for one purpose, Mr. Speaker, namely to point out that in my own riding there would be 200-plus separate polling stations, yet in that whole area there would be not more than four or five advanced polls.
We all want to make it possible for the greatest number of people to vote on polling day. We want the voters to realize that it is their duty to vote. But if they cannot vote on voting day, nobody in this parliament is depriving them of the right to vote. They are prevented from voting because of some domestic factor or some factor such as work, business, pleasure or vacation. They have
Canada Elections Act
to choose between the two, whether the right to vote is of sufficient importance to forgo the other or vice versa.
My objection to this bill is based on the fact that I do not see how it can be applied on a practicable basis to my riding, which is similar to all the ridings in my province, and similar as well to ridings in other parts of Canada, particularly British Columbia. I submit that if this house is going to provide extra convenience for one set of voters in one locality then, by the same token, we must provide the same conveniences for other voters in other localities wherever they may live. I believe it was the hon. member for Regina City who spoke of treating every voter fairly. If we are going to treat every voter fairly, the only way that can be done is to set up advance polls in every community. If we do that we will double or triple the cost of an election. In addition to that, we will be destroying the very meaning of polling day itself. In other words, the result of this bill would be to destroy the main significance of the election act.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I find myself unable to support this bill. My argument is this. Why should a person be granted an extra convenience just because he happens to live in a certain place, because he lives in a large centre or because he works in an industrial centre? Surely every voter has equal rights under the law. He has equal rights because this parliament has given him the same conveniences that we grant to all others. Unless this bill envisages setting up advance polls at every polling station in Canada, then it discriminates against the places where advance polls are not set up.
That is the very thing this bill claims to do, to eliminate discrimination, but all it will do will be to increase the discrimination. The only way discrimination can be avoided is to set up advance polls in every polling station in Canada. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that is impracticable, and for that reason I cannot support the bill.

vote on polling day. Let us ask, first, who is going to determine whether or not each individual is right or wrong in the belief that he cannot vote on polling day. This is quite a complication. Who is going to decide that Mr. So and So is right in believing six or seven days before the polling date, that he cannot vote on election day? In my opinion that is quite a weak spot in the bill.
The second weak spot is that in my estimation this bill will create quite a few legal problems. After the last election we did not receive many petitions. In the rural districts we have no problem about voting on polling day, but the problem is greater in the cities, and that is where we now get the trouble on election day. If people are entitled to decide for themselves that they are going to vote at one of the advance polls, then on polling day who is going to decide whether or not the vote was properly given at the advance poll? It will require closer checking in order to avoid duplication of votes. This would open the door to many petitions after the election.
I would think that voting is a duty, and when the date is set by parliament I believe it is a duty that is dear to the heart of every Canadian. I would conclude by saying that the bill, instead of reinforcing the election act, will have just the opposite effect and will destroy an act which has been giving good results. Nearly 70 per cent of the people cast their ballots at the last election, and if we compare this percentage with the percentage of votes cast in many other democratic countries we will see that it is a very good result. I do not see why we should change a law which has been giving such good results.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before six
o'clock I was recalling some instances and examples which had been given in the course of the debate of different groups of people whose opportunity to vote might be increased by the amendment. Quite a variety of examples were given. I daresay that in some instances they were well founded and that the effect of the bill would be to enlarge the opportunity of some people to vote. Perhaps the amendment might work in the opposite direction, because it is hard to see just how these things will work out when you are looking at them in the abstract.
I want to speak for a minute about the principle of the bill, which as I see it is the desirability of making it possible for all those entitled to vote to do so. That objective might be achieved in different ways. You might have a method of voting by proxy when the voter himself is unable to appear, or you might extend the number of voting days. Members of this house will not remember it, but I believe in the early days of confederation voting took place by open ballot. Under those circumstances it would have been possible for people to vote without attending the poll because their ballots were open. Voting could have been done by sending in a letter.
There is no question that in our view of government the right to vote is basic. Some people call it a privilege, and in some countries it is regarded as a duty. In those cases those eligible to vote are under some compulsion to cast their ballots whether they want to or not. We have not taken that view in Canada, but undoubtedly this is a basic right and anything within reason which will assist those entitled to exercise it is desirable.
As I understand the proposed amendment, the problem is approached from the point of view of the number of voting days to be made available and the spacing of those days. That is exactly the same principle as the present election act, but with a different arrangement of the days on which one may vote. It is possible to suggest a great many combinations of voting days. Regular voting might take place on more than one day, on a series of days, or there might be two periods for voting as under the present act. There

Canada Elections Act
are various arrangements of those two periods by placing them at greater or lesser intervals apart.
I think it is desirable that as far as possible all people who wish to exercise their franchise should do so at as nearly the same time as can be arranged conveniently, so that all will be casting their ballots on the same issues with the same considerations before them. It is not often that election issues change very much from day to day, but one can recall instances where the results of elections have been changed by reason of something that has happened in the last day or two of the campaign. As a general approach it seems to me desirable that as far as possible everyone should vote at almost the same time. Therefore I would not think it wise to have an advance poll some distance ahead of the regular poll.
The other question involved is who should be entitled to take advantage of these advance polls. This is the broadest suggestion of its kind that has been submitted, because it goes almost as far as saying that anyone who considers it would be convenient to vote at an advance poll rather than waiting for the ordinary voting day could persuade himself to that effect and make his affidavit reasonably near the fact by saying that he had reason to believe he would not be able to vote later, and govern himself accordingly.
I think it is admitted that the present category of those who are entitled to vote at the advance poll is fairly narrow. I have known of people whose business took them away regularly and who did not fall within the limited categories named, though they were on a par with those who were entitled to use the advance poll. It appears to me that the categories as now enumerated might very well be enlarged in order to make it unnecessary for anyone whose ordinary course of business took him away from his polling division on voting day to be denied the opportunity of casting his ballot at an advance poll.
When one tries to go beyond that and suggest that being on holidays is a good reason for not attending to vote, it seems to me that a very wide net is being spread to catch a very few voters. My experience is that people who are away on holidays do not like to be interrupted. As a matter of fact, in our exercise of the franchise in this country at all levels of government the proportion of those who see fit to exercise their voting right is lamentably small. In elections in the city in which my constituency is located as few as 25 per cent of the qualified voters have turned up on occasion to cast

their ballots. That perhaps is extreme. I think on the average some 50 per cent see fit to go to the poll and vote.	.
Of course these are non-party elections. With the help of the political parties a good many voters are stimulated to go to the poll and cast their votes. That creates more interest, with the result that in provincial and dominion elections, in my experience, the percentage of the qualified electorate voting ranges from 54 or 55 per cent to as much as 90 per cent in some polling subdivisions. Now it is a question whether the system can be improved. I have mentioned the case of people on holidays. They are not anxious to disturb their vacation, as a general rule, and though some of them will go long distances to vote others would not take advantage of the advance poll even if it were set up for them.
