As I have already said, I rise at this time to give my full support to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Beauce. Might I point out at this time that Canada is the home of French Canadians, and I believe they should be made to feel at home from the shores of the Atlantic to the shores of the Pacific. Together we of French Canadian origin and those of English speaking origin can build Canada into a great nation.
Might I point out that the only reason we have a confederation instead of a unitary state is because of the French Canadians. We asked them to come into confederation as full partners with English speaking Canadians, yet at the same time we wanted to preserve their rights and their own way of life. We divided authority between the federal government and the provinces primarily so the French speaking people would not be overwhelmed by the English speaking majority.
Might I point out that in the province where I live and where I was born the English speaking minority are perfectly free to live their own way of life and teach their own mother tongue. Their schools have been well provided for since confederation by each provincial government which happened to be in power, regardless of its political

Financial Administration Act make-up. I should like to point out also that in Quebec nine out of every ten people are of the Roman Catholic faith, with eight out of every ten speaking the French language. Yet the minority have complete autonomy and equality.
There may be some hon. members of the house, and I am thinking particularly of those who come from distant parts of Canada, who question the need for the legislation proposed by the hon. member in Bill No. 6. Indeed, it would not be strange if some of those whose lives have been spent in British Columbia, for example, where the French language is rarely heard, were inclined to make light of the proposal in Bill No. 6.
To those hon. members, if any there be, I should like to point out some rather surprising figures, or at least I think they will be surprising to them, and I refer to the tabulations resulting from the dominion census of 1951. In that year the total population was just over 14 million people, and of that total 2,741,812 used the French language as their only means of communication with one another. I do not quote that figure in any disparaging way, any more than I would disparage the more than nine million Canadians who according to that census spoke only English. I merely call it to the attention of the house to illustrate my point that a very considerable number of the people in this country speak French exclusively.
They have every right to do so, because the right of Canadians to the use of the French language is inviolate. The British North America Act contains guarantees in this respect with which I am sure all hon. members are familiar. I submit that those who framed our written constitution did not mean or intend that the use of the French language should be limited to the federal parliament, the federal courts, the Quebec legislative assembly and the courts of Quebec. In 1867, when a French speaking minority was entering somewhat fearfully into a new kind of political partnership with the English speaking majority, it was thought necessary, and I believe rightly so, to guarantee the areas in which the use of the French language would be of the greatest value to the minority. This, you might say, was the irreducible minimum.
From that starting point I think one must assume that several factors govern the determination of whether English or French shall be used in the official business of government or the day to day business of living, and by far the most important factor is the ability of those communicating with one another to understand the same language.


I come now to the 2.75 million Canadians whose only language is French. The question here is not on the high plane of constitutional rights, it is on the very practical level of communication. The only way to address them and be understood is in the French language. Whenever the federal government has to communicate with them, in respect to income tax for example, it does so in French. That is only practical common sense.

No argument need be advanced in favour of this bill. On the contrary, it should be carried without the slightest delay. It is based on principles which are fundamental in Canada. I feel, like many other Canadians, that statements of principle would tend to be lowered to the level of electoral considerations if some legislation did not occasionally confirm the feelings so eloquently expressed about national unity. It is sometimes said that we must rely on public opinion since it is the safest guide and that the task of enforcing such measures must be left to public opinion and not to parliament. However, I do not believe that this dangerous argument can be applied in any way to this bill. A matter which goes right down to the soul of a nation, such as official bilingualism, leaves no ground for discussion. When the tradition, the history and the constitution of our country are at stake, we have no alternative but to respect them without discussion.
This bill is based on these sacred rights; to reject it would not be simply to repudiate what we are but it would be a crime of lese-majesty.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few observations to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard), who, at the beginning of his remarks told us that there was only 25 minutes left to discuss the bill, and that we should not speak about it until ten o'clock, because that would mean a first class funeral.
I wish to tell him that we all have a right to express our views about the bill which, if it is not carried today, will stay on the order paper, just like all other bills, and as the house will sit again in the coming weeks, members will have other opportunities to study it.
There is no need to rush matters. We are here to express our opinions, and I suggest that it is not by rushing things that we will be able to discuss them freely. I have listened to the arguments expressed by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) in support of that measure, and I must congratulate him on the serious motives he brought in support of this proposal.


Since we have in this country bilingual postage stamps and money why should it not be the same for cheques and negotiable instruments issued by the government? What is asked for in this bill is nothing more than simple logic. If certain instruments within the jurisdiction of the federal government are bilingual, why should it not be the same in all cases.
Bilingualism has a purpose and it is a well known fact that it has constantly progressed in Canada and that its use is helping the cause of national unity.
We are trying to teach the younger generation the double culture which gives its vitality to our country, by teaching the French language to the young English speaking Canadians, and the English language to the young French speaking Canadians. Why do we see those young students from French universities fraternize with their fellow students of the English universities? Why do we see the students from English provinces spend their holidays in the province of Quebec in order to learn French, and those from Quebec go to the English provinces in order to improve their knowledge of the English language? All this is done in order to develop bilingualism and cement understanding and goodwill between both racial groups of our country. If we have such movements, it is because the Canadian people understand the characteristics of bilingualism and want it to carry its full effect.
When we see crown corporations give evidence of bilingualism as do the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority lay issuing bilingual cheques, we cannot help congratulating their officials for their attitude and telling them that they show a great understanding of their responsibilities toward the Canadian people.
Under those circumstances, it is easy to see that the Canadian people want bilingualism to develop and increase in this country; therefore I support wholeheartedly the measure introduced by the hon. member for Beauce.
The hon. member has shown us that bilingual postage stamps and money had been prejudicial to no one, and that the issuing of bilingual cheques wil not affect the rights or privileges of any Canadian, but that, on the contrary, it will help the cause of national unity.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join the previous speakers in extending congratulations and thanks to the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) for being so tenacious in presenting this bill which, I am sure, has as much significance for his constituents as it has for my own constituents.

Since I have been sitting in this house I have often noted that we can all have the same object in view but hold different opinions as to the best manner in which to attain it.
The purpose of this bill is to cement Canadian unity in providing that all Canadian citizens, when they get a cheque from Her Majesty, will get it printed in both languages. I see no more objection to that than in the case of a money order printed in both the official languages of the country.
We of the province of Quebec have only to go back to the past to realize that we deem it somewhat important to have cheques and money orders or any document whatsoever from the federal treasury printed in both languages. French and English are the two official languages in this country.
I find some interesting statistics in pamphlet no. 84 from the information division of the External Affairs Department, based on a text of Charles Bilodeau of Laval University, Quebec city.
As a matter of fact, to refer to my own little home county in lower Quebec, French has been spoken there from 1608 to 1759. For this reason, it will easily be understood that atavism or devotion to our tradition demands expression in the beloved language of those who founded that part of the country. After 1760, there was an increase in population either by natural growth or by immigration.

If you consider what took place after the treaty of Paris, on the surrender of New1 France to England, you find that there is nothing explicit on the language of the people of this country; still the use of French persisted. In 1774, the Quebec Act restored the French Civil Code and authorized the use of the French language before the courts.
In 1791, Canada was made up of Lower Canada and Upper Canada. In Lower Canada, that is in Quebec, the elected members of the legislature decided to use both languages in their debates as well as for the publication of the statutes and of related documents.
In 1840, the Act of Union stated that the English language would be the only official language of parliament but that, on the-other hand, the statutes would be translated into French. However, in spite of that rule,, a francophile member delivered a speech in French in the house and the use of the French language became more frequent such as is the case today.
In 1867, the Canadian confederation was set up. The constitution of the new nation was then incorporated into the British North America Act whose section 133 reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this Act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
The statutes of the House of Commons are printed in both languages. Besides, the official record of debates is published in both the official languages. Why then not print all cheques and instruments from the treasury department in both official languages?
If we look at what is going on in our schools, for instance in the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, we see, as is apparent from a reading of the document to which I referred a moment ago, that there are 1,175 French-speaking classes in New Brunswick, 205 in Nova Scotia and 75 in Prince Edward Island.
To my mind, the printing of all official documents in the two languages would in no way reduce the necessity or the usefulness for each and everyone of us to understand both languages.
Over the last few years we have been in a position to observe remarkable progress

Financial Administration Act towards bilingualism in this country. In fact in some of our institutions French and English are generally placed on the same footing. Most French Canadian parents wish their children to have a practical knowledge of the language of the majority. Associations are promoting bilingualism by means of visits to the various provinces which make up the Canadian confederation.
Mr. Speaker for all the reasons which I have just given, I am happy to associate myself with the hon. member for Beauce and to congratulate him on having presented this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us proposes to amend chapter 116 of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1952 so that in the future all negotiable instruments enumerated in section 33 shall be printed in the two official languages its effect to extend to all departments and crown corporations as defined in section 76 (1) (c). I congratulate the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) for his initiative in introducing this bill. In so doing, he not only reaches at the purest source of liberalism but he undoubtedly answers the desire of the great majority of Canadian citizens.
It is mere common sense that negotiable instruments issued by the Canadian government be bilingual. If everywhere today people take pleasure in pointing out the dual culture of Canada, it seems to me that it is only logical that the government be the first to recognize everywhere and forever the reality of bilingualism by issuing bilingual cheques as soon as possible.
In declaring myself in favour of this legislation, I am far from feeling as if I were seeking a privilege, for even though bilingualism at the national level is not expressly recognized in the act of confederation the point here is whether a right should be recognized. As a matter of fact, the constitution must not be read in a restrictive way but rather in its broadest meaning in order to promote throughout Canada a spirit of understanding and good feeling between the two great races which make up our nation. It is unfortunate that we feel obliged to raise these questions from time to time and I believe that we will always deserve credit for doing so very carefully. We must do it, nevertheless, for the great difficulty is not misunderstanding but rather the lack of a clear and accurate text.

I must say here that the Liberal party has been doing from time immemorial more than its share to straighten out this defect in our constitution.
Mr. Speaker, it was in 1936, under a Liberal government, that a bilingual character was given to our money. Since then, various federal organizations like the St. Lawrence Seav/ay Authority and the C.B.C. have already issued bilingual cheques. We also now have a bilingual stamp. All we have to do now is to make official what custom has already consecrated in various departments. I am therefore in favour of a legislation which, I believe, today meets with no opposition from any part of our people. And I may well make this comment, Mr. Speaker, because I am representing a riding where perhaps a little more than a third of the population is English-speaking. I know that such legislation is popular with us, for both races are doing their best to get along together. Moreover, it is by making concessions that we shall succeed in bettering this mutual understanding.
I recognize that the implementation of this piece of legislation may run into some difficulties at the administrative level. But I rely on the understanding of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to eliminate those difficulties, to get around them, so that, right from this year, the negotiable instruments issued by the government may be bilingual.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to dwell on this matter at greater length. I notice it is 10 o'clock and so I move the adjournment of the debate.
